title: Florence CO Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Florence well records show a 55-foot median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and fractured-bedrock drilling costs from $9,600.
h1: What Florence, Colorado Well Records Tell You
intro_html:
Buying land near Florence means looking past the home and checking the water record. Permits within 5 miles show a wide range of well conditions: the median recorded depth is 55 feet, but some wells reach 2,180 feet. Most permitted wells are domestic or household wells, and the local records primarily identify fractured bedrock rather than a named Denver Basin aquifer.

That combination matters when comparing lots in Florence, Rockvale, Williamsburg, Brookside, and nearby Fremont County areas. A shallow well may be economical, but depth and production can vary sharply from one parcel to the next. Use the nearby permit data as a planning guide, not a guarantee.

sections.heading: Florence well depth depends on the ground beneath the lot
sections.html:
Recorded wells near Florence have a median depth of 55 feet. The middle half runs from 32 to 180 feet, which gives a driller a useful local range but not a promised target. Sixty-one percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 19% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 11% are 300 to 600 feet, and 9% exceed 600 feet.

The spread reflects mountain ground identified on permits mainly as unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Granite and gneiss can change quickly across a property, with water-bearing fractures appearing at different depths. For a bid, ask the driller to price the expected hole depth separately from casing, grout, pump, and other completion work. A 55-foot median is useful for budgeting, but it should not be treated as a drilling limit.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Florence
sections.html:
Among the Florence-area records that report pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Half of reported wells fall in the 5-to-15-gpm range, and 31% report more than 15 gpm. Eighteen percent report between 1 and 5 gpm, while 2% are under 1 gpm.

Only 124 wells report a pump yield, so the percentages describe reported tests rather than every permitted well. For a buyer, the main concern is dependable household supply during peak use, not just a strong short test. Request the well construction report, pumping test, storage details, and any production history. A low-yield well can sometimes work with storage, but that adds equipment and operating considerations.

sections.heading: Water levels and the record over time
sections.html:
Only 22 Florence-area records report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. In those records, the median depth to water is 22 feet, with the middle half from 20 to 29 feet. That suggests relatively shallow measured water levels in the reported wells, but it does not establish the water level for every parcel or prove a basin-wide trend.

Permit activity increased from 8 permits in the 1950s to 174 in the 2000s, then shows 111 in the 2010s and 40 in the 2020s. Those are permit counts, not water-level measurements, so they should not be read as evidence that the water table is dropping. Have the driller check nearby completed wells and ask how the proposed location compares with recent construction.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Florence, and when
sections.html:
The permit history reaches back to the 1950s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The records show 783 permitted wells within 5 miles, 452 recorded as constructed, 509 with a total depth, and 124 with a pump yield. That is enough local history to compare nearby construction, but not every permit contains complete completion information.

The most active named drillers in the records are Finney Drilling, listed as Finney, Larry D., with 74 records; Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, with 71; and Arkansas Valley Drilling, listed as Moore, Todd A., with 69. Treat those counts as permit-record history, not endorsements or proof that a company is currently available. Ask for current licensing, insurance, references, and a written scope before choosing a driller.

sections.heading: What a new Florence well may cost
sections.html:
Local ground is modeled as fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The drilling rate used for this area is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,600 to $5,500. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,600 to $17,500 at the median depth. A deeper hole can move well beyond that range, and a fractured-rock site may need additional work if the first interval does not produce enough water. Get the assumed depth, casing and grout, pump size, trench length, electrical work, testing, and permit-related tasks written into the bid so estimates can be compared fairly.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Florence
sections.html:
Water quality deserves a separate review from well quantity. Within about 10 miles, mapped environmental information includes 32 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 62 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not automatically mean a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to check the parcel, nearby land uses, and available agency records.

Low yield, dry holes, and fractured-rock variability are the practical drilling risks. Septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, driveway access, and building placement also need to be checked before selecting a well location. A domestic permit does not eliminate the need to verify what the permit allows. Have water tested after construction and again when a property history or nearby environmental feature warrants it.

sections.heading: A sensible Florence lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Before closing, pull the permits for the property and compare them with nearby wells in Florence, Rockvale, Williamsburg, and Brookside. Look for completed depth, yield, static water level, casing information, and the actual use listed on the permit. The local use mix is 68% domestic or household, 17% stock, 4% irrigation, and 19% monitoring, so not every nearby well is a good comparison for a residence.

For a vacant lot, make the well location, septic area, access route, and electrical path part of the feasibility review. Have a licensed driller inspect the geology and price a realistic depth range instead of relying only on the 55-foot median. If the parcel depends on an exempt household-use well, confirm the current permit conditions and allowed uses with Colorado DWR before designing the home.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Florence, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Florence is 55 feet, and the middle half runs from 32 to 180 feet. Sixty-one percent are under 100 feet, but the deepest recorded well reaches 2,180 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can change quickly, so nearby records guide a bid but cannot guarantee your lot’s depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Florence, CO?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 55-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,600 to $5,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,600 to $17,500. A deeper or difficult fractured-bedrock hole can cost more.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Florence?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0-gpm median, with the middle half from 5.0 to 15.0 gpm. Half of reported wells are in the 5-to-15-gpm range, while 2% report under 1 gpm. Only 124 records report yield, so ask for the specific well’s test and production history.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Florence, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Within about 10 miles, records map 32 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 62 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These do not prove contamination at your parcel. Test the well after construction and review nearby environmental records before relying on it for drinking water.

faq.q: Are Florence wells in the Denver Basin aquifer?
faq.a: No Denver Basin aquifer wells are identified in the Florence permit records. The records name 748 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, 14 in alluvial aquifer, and 5 in the Dakota Group Aquifer. That fractured-bedrock setting can produce very different depths and yields between neighboring properties, so parcel-specific records and a driller’s review matter.
